When something spurts, it shoots out suddenly, with force, in a quick, pressured stream. Think of pressing your thumb against a garden hose — the water doesn't just flow out gently; it shoots out in a fast, forceful burst. That's spurting.

The word carries three key qualities at once: suddenness, pressure/force, and briefness. Something that spurts doesn't trickle slowly, and it doesn't pour steadily for a long time — it bursts out in a quick, energetic rush.

Sense 1 — A liquid (or substance) shoots out suddenly

This is the most common use. When a liquid spurts, it is ejected or released with force, usually from a small opening, under pressure.

  • When he cut his finger deeply, blood spurted from the wound.
  • She squeezed the ketchup bottle too hard and it spurted all over the table.
  • The cracked pipe spurted water across the basement floor.
  • He bit into the ripe tomato and juice spurted down his chin.

Notice in all these cases: the liquid isn't calmly dripping or gently flowing — it's shooting out with some force, quickly, in a stream.

This sense can work in two ways grammatically:

  • The liquid itself spurts: Blood spurted from the cut. (The blood is doing the spurting.)
  • Something causes liquid to spurt: The hose spurted water everywhere. (The hose is causing the water to shoot out.)

Both are perfectly natural.

Sense 2 — A person, animal, or vehicle suddenly moves fast for a short time

Here, "spurt" describes a sudden short burst of speed or acceleration — moving ahead quickly for a brief moment, usually in the context of a race, competition, or chase.

  • In the final stretch of the race, she spurted ahead and crossed the finish line first.
  • The rabbit spurted forward the moment it sensed the fox approaching.
  • The car spurted past us and disappeared around the corner.
  • He had been jogging at a steady pace, but spurted when he saw the finish line.

The key here is that the movement is sudden and temporary — a short, sharp burst, not a sustained, long-distance sprint. After a spurt of speed, a person might slow back down.
What Makes "Spurt" Different From Similar Words

Since "spurt" lives in a neighbourhood of words that all describe liquid or fast movement, it's important to know exactly where it sits among them.

Spurt vs. drip: When something drips, it falls in slow, separate drops — no force, no speed, no stream. Spurting is the opposite energy entirely.

Spurt vs. flow: Flow is smooth, steady, and continuous — like a river flowing. Spurting is abrupt and pressured, not calm or continuous.

Spurt vs. gush: Gush involves a large, dramatic rush of liquid — a big volume pouring out rapidly. Spurting is more focused and narrower. A burst pipe might gush water; a punctured vein spurts blood. Gushing tends to be more generous in volume; spurting is sharper and more jet-like.

Spurt vs. squirt: These two are very close, and in everyday use people often use them interchangeably. However, squirt usually emphasises a thin, directed, intentional stream (you squirt a water gun at someone deliberately). Spurt more often implies something happening suddenly, sometimes with less control, under pressure — it can feel more accidental or forceful. Blood spurts; you squirt lemon juice onto fish.

Spurt vs. spray: Spray scatters liquid in many directions at once — like a sprinkler or a sneeze. Spurting is a single stream, not a scattered mist.

"Spurt" has a slightly visceral, physical feel to it. It often appears in contexts involving the body (blood, sweat, saliva, juice), machines under pressure (pipes, hoses, engines), and athletic competition (running, racing). It's not a gentle or elegant word — it suggests rawness, pressure, and a lack of complete control. Things that spurt often do so because something built up and then released, or because something was squeezed or broken.

Less commonly, "spurt" can describe a sudden brief increase in something abstract — activity, growth, or interest — that mirrors the idea of a short burst of energy.

  • The economy spurted briefly after the tax cuts, then slowed again.
  • His motivation spurted at the start of the project but faded quickly.

This usage is much less frequent than the physical senses, but you may encounter it.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

To spurt is to shoot out suddenly and forcefully in a stream (liquid) or to move suddenly fast for a short time (speed). The word always implies something brief, pressured, and abrupt — never slow, gentle, or sustained.
